newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO battles on as temperatures plunge in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: NATO battles on as temperatures plunge in Bosnia.

text.p: NATO troops fighting to rebuild Bosnia after a shattering 43-month war now have to battle one of the worst winters of the 20th century in Europe.
Logistical headaches abound -- helicopters grounded in the snow, mountain satellite stations marooned in blizzards, landslides and crashed lorries blocking major highways.

"It is certainly more difficult to move troops around. We haven't been stopped but we have been disrupted," said Brigadier David Leakey at the headquarters in northern town of Banja Luka of the British troops with NATO's Stabilisation Force.
The 31,000 troops with a mandate over the next 18 months to try and keep the peace in a land ravaged by war have to deal with temperatures that plunge to minus 30 degrees Centigrade at night.
Acknowledging that Bosnia along with much of Europe has been hit by the worst winter of the century, Leakey said: "We have had huge difficulties supplying hilltop rebroadcasting stations.
"It has limited our ability at times to carry on with our patrols, particularly in remote villages. Some of these villages are living on subsistence and we do alert the aid agencies."
Troops working on one communications centre in Viterog, a 2,000-metre peak now swathed in snow, have been marooned up there for more than two weeks.

"Helicopters cannot get into them because of the low cloud and it is very difficult to clear safely the tracks leading up to them," Leakey said at the British headquarters, now housed in a cavernous metal factory.
"We have had no physical contact with them for the last two weeks," he said of the marooned team.
But many apparently enjoy the solitary life up in the mountains with reports of teams befriending wild horses and adopting pet dogs in their hillside hideaways.
Five British soldiers have died in road accidents in Bosnia while three were killed by mines.

The cold has not killed anyone yet but Leakey said that temperatures for the last two to three weeks have been minus 15 Celsius (5 Fahrenheit) throughout the day, plummeting to minus 30 Celsius (minus 22 Fahrenheit) at night.
Two helicopters have been forced to make unscheduled landings. A jacknifed lorry blocked one road, engineers had to move in to clear a landslide from another.
The weather certainly dealt a blow to the latest visit to Bosnia by British Defence Minister Michael Portillo.
His official plane was diverted to Zagreb and his convoy had to drive in by road in a whiteout. It was impossible to visit some units on a day when the horizon was invisible in the gloom.
But there is one positive side to the atrocious weather -- it keeps the lid on hatred that might bubble over anytime among the ethnic communities.
"When cold sets in, it puts a wet blanket over the ardour of the factions to make trouble," Leakey told reporters.
